# General

### Welcome to COMP0005 Algorithms

This Moodle course is the central point of your Connected Learning experience for COMP0005 Algorithms and contains key module and assessment information, course materials, and all learning activities.

- `url` **COMP0005 module description** — moduleId: `8525788` — [open](https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/mod/url/view.php?id=8525788)

  UCL’s Module Catalogue provides summary information for all modules running at the University in the current academic year.

#### Key Module Information

##### Aims

The aim of this module is to provide students with an introduction to data structures and algorithms that are fundamental to programming and to understand computation. We will apply these techniques to computational problems, with the aim to develop problem-solving skills, to develop the ability to analyse the efficiency of algorithms, and to encourage a thoughtful approach to the analysis and design of computational problems.

##### Learning outcomes

On successful completion of the module, a student will be able to:

- Understand a variety of fundamental data structures and be able to use them effectively in the design and implementation of algorithms;
- Understand a variety of fundamental algorithmic problems and algorithms for solving them;
- Analyse the space and time efficiency of algorithms and understand how to design efficient algorithms.

##### Content

The course will cover:

- Fundamentals of algorithms and data structures
- Sorting Algorithms
- Searching Algorithms
- Graphs Algorithms
- String-processing Algorithms

There will be an emphasis on the application of these data structures and algorithms to solve computational problems.

#### Module Overview

We provide two one-hour lectures and one two-hour practical lab session each week. The lectures will be recorded through Panopto, although you are encouraged to attend in person wherever possible.

##### Requisites

All students on this module are expected to have basic experience of programming in [Python](https://www.python.org/) and of using [Jupyter Notebook](https://jupyter.org/). If you are new to either (or both), please make use of the many freely available online resources and tutorials for self-study; your Programming Tutor may also provide additional support.

##### Textbook

[Algorithms, 4th edition](https://algs4.cs.princeton.edu/home/)
By Robert Sedgewick and Kevin Wayne
Published by Addison-Wesley Professional (March 24, 2011) © 2011

##### Labs and Coursework

All practicals and coursework use [Python 3](https://www.python.org/) and [Jupyter Notebook](https://jupyter.org/) as the primary programming and computing platforms, respectively.

#### Formative Assessment and Developmental Learning

Formative assessment and developmental learning activities are designed to help you succeed in your summative assessments. For this module, you will undertake programming and algorithm design exercises, intended to be carried out in the weekly computer lab sessions as well as in self-study outside class.

#### Accessibility

#### Digital Accessibility Statement

UCL is committed to equity of opportunity for all students, including those with disabilities and specific learning difficulties. We are working to improve the digital accessibility of our learning resources and platforms, but recognise that some resources provided may not currently be accessible to all students.

- In this course we provide a range of resources in Word, PowerPoint, and PDF format which are keyboard navigable accessible to students using a screen reader.
- Alternative formats are available on demand using Blackboard Ally. [Ally works to convert common file types to other formats](https://wiki.ucl.ac.uk/x/dAZXBw) automatically and in line with the original file. These alternatives include audio (mp3), PDF, ePub for eReaders, or Braille reader files.
- If you require an accessible version (e.g. an alternative format) of any of the resources used in this module that is not provided by Ally, please contact module staff.

# General

### Welcome to COMP0002 Principles of Programming

#### An Introduction to Programming

#### using the C and Haskell Programming Languages

This Moodle site contains the information you need to take the module. It's where you'll find key module and assessment information, the weekly content, links to other materials, and the exercise questions, and coursework information. The weekly content will be added progressively as the module runs.

#### Module Overview

The official module syllabus, in the UCL Module Catalogue, can be [viewed here](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/module-catalogue/modules/principles-of-programming/COMP0002). The syllabus lists the content and learning outcomes for the module.

#### Module Timeline

The module runs in Term 1, 5th October 2026 to 18th December 2026. There is no teaching or lab classes in Reading Week (9-13th November 2026).

COMP0002 has two parts:

- Part I during the first five weeks of term 1 introduces **imperative programming using C**, taught by [Prof. Graham Roberts](mailto:graham.roberts@ucl.ac.uk). (weeks 6-10, 5th October 2026 to 6th November 2026)
-

Part II during the last five weeks of term 1 introduces **functional programming using Haskell**, taught by [Dr. David Clark](http://david.clark@ucl.ac.uk). (weeks 12-16, 16th November 2026 to 18th December 2026)

#### Lectures

There are three timetabled lecture hours per week, delivered as one two-hour lecture and one one-hour lecture. See your personal timetable for the times and locations. Subject to any updates the lectures are in person on campus, but will be recorded via Panopto. It is expected that you will attend all lectures in person, and will need to use your id card to touch in and record your attendance.

#### Labs

Labs are where you get help and feedback from the Teaching Assistants (TAs) for the programming exercises. There are multiple lab groups, and you are allocated to _one_ of the groups (not all of them!). You are expected to attend your group's two-hour lab class each week, which will be the one you see in your personal timetable. There are ten teaching weeks, hence ten labs to attend overall, with no labs during Reading Week.

### FAQs

If the answer isn't here then post a message to the Q&A Forum.

1._I don’t know where to start!_

Get a very basic, simplified version of the program working first, then extend it step by step. For example, first work out how to display the background tile grid. Display the maze using lines and squares, with a value used to represent the content of each square (wall, empty, entrance, exit marker).

2. _How do you position the robot and walls in the maze?_The simplest way is to just put code in the program to position everything, but this has the disadvantage of having to edit and recompile to change any of the positions. Better would be to either use command line arguments or read a data file, or a combination of both, to input the positions so that the program code does not need to change.

3. _Do I have to write complicated code so that the robot can always find the exit, wherever anything is positioned?_Avoid making your code complicated, simpler is better! If you complete all the stages then the exit should always be found, providing the positioning of walls doesn't make it impossible. Work through the stages step-by-step in small increments as far as you can.

4. _The robot is moving so fast I can't see what is happening!_
Use the sleep function: void sleep(int milliseconds). Calling the function will pause the animation for the number of milliseconds specified, e.g., sleep(1000) will sleep for 1 second (1000 milliseconds). Sleeping for 100-300 milliseconds is probably good enough, as you still want the robot to move fairly quickly.

5. _The Close Window button on the drawing window doesn't respond._
Type Ctrl-c (hold the control key down and press c) to stop the program.

6. _The size of my .zip directory containing the finished coursework exceeds the Moodle upload size limit._

Your zip file is way too large, it should typically only be a few hunderd kilobytes in size at the most! You have probably added compiled code or other large files by mistake. You do, however, need to include any data or image/icon files needed to run the program.

_7. Can I upload a text file containing the URL from which the .zip directory can be safely downloaded (e.g. my OneDrive storage)?_

No, you should must upload the source code + documentation in the .zip file to Moodle, plus any data files or image files needed to run the program.

7. _What is good practice for code comments?_

Comments should be kept minimal and should always **add** information that is not apparent from reading the code. The code itself should be as readable as possible, with variables and functions having clear descriptive names, and good layout used. In general, comments are a liability as they need to be kept synchronised with the code as it is edited, and can easily get out of date.

You should consider comments for:

- References/citations to other work you are making use of.
- Where necessary, providing more information about the design or use of an algorithm, minimising the dependencies on specific lines or versions of code.

If you think a comment is needed to explain a complicated section of code, then make the code more readable! One way of doing this is to split the code into a collection of smaller functions, where each function has a clear name that explains its purpose.

Never include comments like "this is a variable called length", or any that repeat what the code says. Don't provide big multi-line blocks of comments, or use comments to break up source code files into sections (use multiple source code files instead).

8. _Can I use additional code libraries that are not part of the standard C library?_

No, you should just use the standard C libraries that come with the compiler, and the DrawApp graphics.h and graphics.c files. Any other code you need you have to write yourself. You should not need anything extra anyway!

Your code must compile and run using the standard gcc or clang installation without any additions, except graphics.h/c.

#### Key Module Information

- `url` **Module description** — moduleId: `8625361` — [open](https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/mod/url/view.php?id=8625361)

  UCL’s Module Catalogue provides summary information for all modules running at the University in the current academic year. To view the summary of this module enter the module code or keywords from its title.

#### Module Overview

The module aims to equip first year computer science students with knowledge of foundational mathematics and logic that will be needed for future computer science modules. To provide students with basic tools and skills for mathematical problem solving, proof and refutation.

Students are provided with weekly problem sheets and attend weekly problem classes to work through the problems.

COMP0147 introduces the mathematical foundations essential for computer science, focusing on formal reasoning, proof techniques, and discrete structures. The module combines theoretical understanding with practical applications, helping students develop the precision and logical thinking required in computing.

Teaching will take place through a mix of lectures, problem-solving classes, and guided exercises. Lectures will introduce key ideas, definitions, and theorems, while the problem sheets will reinforce understanding through hands-on practice and collaborative discussion. Students will be encouraged to reason carefully, write clear proofs, and connect abstract concepts to computational examples.

The module is organised into thematic blocks:

-

**Week 1: Logic** – Propositional Logic, Applications of Propositional Logic, logical equivalence, Predicates and Quantifiers, Rules of Inference.

-

**Week 2: Proofs** – Introduction to Proofs, Proof Methods and Strategy, Introduction to number theory: Divisibility and Modular Arithmetic, Primes and Greatest Common Divisors.

-

**Week 3: Sets & Functions** – Sets, Set Operations, Functions.

-

**Week 4: Sets & Functions** – Sequences and Summations, Cardinality of Sets, Foundations of Mathematics.

-

**Week 5: Induction** – Mathematical Induction, Strong Induction and Well-Ordering.

-

**Week 6: Recursion**– Recursive Definitions and Structural Induction, Recursive Algorithms, Program Correctness.

-

**Week 7: Counting** – Combinatorial methods including permutations, combinations, binomial coefficients, and the inclusion–exclusion principle.

-

**Week 8: Relations** – Equivalence relations, partial orders, and graphical representations.

-

**Weeks 9–10: Graph Theory** – Graphs, paths, cycles, trees, colourings, and planar graphs.

#### Formative Assessment and Developmental Learning

Formative assessment and developmental learning activities are designed to help you succeed in your summative assessments. Throughout the module, you will complete weekly exercises designed to develop your understanding of discrete mathematics and your ability to construct rigorous mathematical proofs. Lectures and Problem Solving sessions provide opportunities to discuss solutions, ask questions, and receive feedback from teaching staff. Practice quizzes and additional exercises are also provided to help you identify areas for improvement and prepare for the final examination.

All new UCL students are required to complete Active Bystander training during the first few weeks of Term 1. It is a core part of your induction and time at UCL.

As a **core part of your induction and time at UCL**, you are **expected** to complete the **[Active Bystander Programme](https://studentsunionucl.org/active-bystander-programme)** which consists of:

- A 30-40 min **[online module](https://studentsunionucl.org/course/active-bystander-programme-online-module)** (to be completed before attending this workshop)
- A **90-minute live workshop.** Your allocated workshop is appearing in your [UCL Timetable](https://timetable.ucl.ac.uk/tt/homePage.do) (also visible in the [UCL Go App](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/isd/services/websites-apps/ucl-go)) in academic Week 5, 6, 7 or 8.

The programme, which has trained over 50,000 students, empowers you to recognise and challenge bullying, harassment, discrimination, and sexual misconduct, helping to build a safe, respectful and inclusive community for all.

By completing this training, you will gain:

- Practical tools for safe intervention
- Understanding of support services at UCL
- Skills to support an inclusive academic and social environment
- A certificate upon completion

**This training is a core part of your induction for all new UCL students (2025/26 onwards)**, in line with national requirements to tackle harassment and misconduct in higher education.

**Completion of both parts of this training is required for certification.**

We recognise that some content may be distressing, particularly for those with lived experience. If you're concerned it may impact your wellbeing, you're welcome to email us to discuss opting out of the training. Please email: [activebystander@ucl.ac.uk](mailto:activebystander@ucl.ac.uk)

# General Information - Start Here!

### Before You Start...

#### Structure

Engineering Challenges is a faculty level module as part of the IEP. It is run by the Faculty of Engineering and not any single department. So, Engineering Challenges includes: Biochemical, Chemical, Biomedical, Mechanical, Electronic & Electrical, Computer Science and Civil Engineering. You will work in interdisciplinary teams during Challenge 2.

That means that the **Module Lead, Dr Sam Fishlock**, works within the faculty and not one particular department (although he is primarily a Mechanical Engineer). The Module Lead has ultimate responsibility for the module and everything that happens within it. He reports to the Director of the IEP and the IEP Exam Board.

Usually, the module lead is the person that you see most often in the classroom and would be the main point of contact.

**However, Challenges is an unusual module**. With over 1000 students across 7 departments, it's impossible for the Module Lead to teach every session.

So who is this person that's in your classroom? We have an extra role that you'll only hear about in IEP modules, **Departmental Lead**. Departmental Leads are experts in your discipline and based in your department. In partnership with the Module Lead, they develop content, set and mark assessment and is the person that you'll see in the classroom on a day to day basis.

##### Teamwork, Language and Design Resources

UCL welcomes students from all over the world and with a wide range of backgrounds. Sometimes you are going to find that you need to do a little bit of extra reading or practise to improve your skills and this will make studying here easier.

A few of the common areas that students do extra research and practise in are **Teamwork, Language** and **Design**.

##### Where can I check my marks?

When we are marking an assessment we will lock submission and usually hide the submission box. This allows us to complete the marking process before releasing the marks to you. The marking process can take a while especially given the number of students that take Engineering Challenges (over 1100 students).

We will put a notification in the Announcements forum when we have released marks for a particular assessment. If you see marks before then, they may change as we are still in the marking process. While we aim to avoid significant changes after we release marks, **marks are always provisional until the IEP Exam Board in June 2027 and so marks may change up until then.**

Once marks are released you will be able to see the marks and feedback for an assessment in the submission box. These marks will not include any penalties that have been applied If you want to see all your marks for the Module including any penalties that have been applied as well as your overall mark for the module there are two options. Gradebook is the first option. You can access it by clicking on Grades in the Navigation block at the right-hand side of the Moodle page. The second option is the MyFeedback section of Moodle. For both of these, the Module total will assume a mark of 0 for anything you have not yet completed. So please be aware that the module total will look low part way through the module. We tend to hide assessments that you have not completed or that we have not released marks for.

Do check your marks once they are released. We try to make sure everything is correct before we release marks but with over 6000 individual marks that need to be checked and released plus any penalties or adjustments that need to made to each one of them, the likelihood is that an error will occur at some point.

If you think an error has been made send us a polite email asking us to check and we will investigate. It may take us a little while to sort some issues out – we may need to check some paperwork or consult the regulations.

### Challenge 1 Brief

Produce a short video (2-3 mins) covering the following topics. You will need to research these – we will not tell you about them in great detail. That's a feature not a bug :-)

- Embedded processors like the ESP32 underpin the Internet of Things (IoT)….

- What are the major challenges in the IoT?
- What are the big current markets for IoT technology?

- Will IoT make a difference to society?
- What are the ethical concerns with IoT technologies?
- Show us the ESP32 working. For this:

- Write a program to output the current time on both the serial output of the TTGO T-display and also on its screen. Hint: you could connect to an NTP server using the WiFi connection in order to set the time on the device. You should feel free to use or combine any of the example programs for the ESP32 or TFT_eSPI so long as you say what you did.
- Demonstrate your program working, and explain (briefly!) what you did and how you did it.

This is a lot to fit into 3 minutes, so you will need to think carefully about what you include and how.

#### Submission Boxes

These are the submission boxes for your summative assessments.

**Individual Contribution to Teamwork (IPAC)**

This assessment has three parts. All of these are related to teamwork. The first part involves weekly team meetings within your on-campus workshop. Within each session, you will be given several questions that as a team you need to discuss and answer. The aim here is to give you some of the structure of how teams communicate and what decisions need to be made. This is not the only time your team needs to meet or communicate but it will give you a start. Every week, one member of your team needs to submit your weekly team meeting minutes. This is just a record of what your team discussed. Below is a link to a Microsoft form where you will submit your meeting minutes. All you need to do is fill in the answers to the questions. It doesn't have to be the same team member each week. You should aim to submit them within 48 hours after your on-campus meeting. If your team submits less than 6 weekly meeting minutes by the end of term, a penalty will be applied to all team members' Individual Contribution to Teamwork marks - 10% of the total mark will be deducted.

The second and third parts are linked. At the end of the project, you will be asked to assess the contribution of all team members, including yourself. Your team will decide near the beginning of the project what criteria you will be used to assess the team. As a team, you will need to select 4 criteria from the list below. During your second team meeting, you will have time to discuss which criteria your team will choose. You can make a decision before that meeting if your team wants to. One member of your team needs to submit your choice in the box below by 2 pm Friday 6th November 2026.

At the end of the project, you will use those criteria to assess all team members using the IPAC tool below. IPAC will ask you to rate each member for each criterion as well as provide feedback to them. Remember that you should provide constructive feedback and think about how you would receive any feedback you intend to give. For general tips on how to give and receive feedback see the peer assessment section of the general information for the Individual Video Presentation. You will need to submit your peer assessment by 2 pm Wednesday 23rd December 2026. Standard late penalties apply and non-completion of the peer assessment will count as no submission and you will receive zero marks. For detailed information on how these penalties apply to this assessment please see the Individual Contribution to Teamwork submission box and for general information on penalties and plagiarism please refer to the relevant section of the Assessment Information tab.

# Individual Social Impact Report

### Individual Social Impact Report

#### Welcome to the Individual Social Impact Report!

As engineers, the work we do has a significant impact on the world. There is a reason that UCL Engineering’s motto is Change the World. Think of the impact of cars, vaccines and machine learning. Equally, the world impacts our work. We need to think about the context we are working within. The people we are designing for, where they live and how they do things will affect the technical details of our design. What language do we need to work in? What weather conditions will our design need to withstand? What resources do we have access to?

So as engineers we need ways to think about the impact we have on the world as well as the impact the world has on us and our work. In this assessment, we are going to start looking at different ways we can do this.

During Challenge 2 you will have a workshop where we discuss the social impact of your Challenge 2 project and start working on the Individual Social Impact Report assessment. The workshop will be led by two of: Dr Fiona Truscott, Dr Vivek Ramachandran, Dr Charlotte Maughan Jones and Dr Sam Fishlock.

These will be either Monday afternoon or Wednesday morning, before or after your project workshop. Do check your timetable on this.

# Welcome

### Welcome to Design and Professional Skills

This Moodle course is the central point of your Connected Learning experience for ENGF0034: Design and Professional Skills. It's where you'll find key module and assessment information, weekly videos and other materials, and all learning activities.

Design and Professional Skills aims to teach fundamental professional skills such as technical writing, visualization, ethics, teamwork, and project management along with a practical understanding of engineering design as it applies to Computer Science. As such, the skills are taught from a technical discipline-focussed perspective and the module is arranged into three main areas: communication, teamwork & project management, discipline-specific skills and projects.

By the end of the module, you will:

- Develop broad technical knowlege and understanding of computer science.
- Develop problem solving skills.
- Learn own strengths and weaknesses and best teamworking practices
- Develop an understanding of ethics for engineers in practice
- Develop the ability to write technical documents, visualise data and present according to audience type
- Develop an understanding of how to manage and lead an engineering project

Term 1 computer science elements of this module are led by [Prof. Martin Benning](https://profiles.ucl.ac.uk/95169-martin-benning)

# How to use this course

#### [image: How to use this course page banner]

#### How to use this course

In term 1, most of the activities are taught by Computer Science, but four activities are taught by the Engineering Faculty. The Computer Science activities can be found in the [Computer Science tab,](https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=60820&section=3) while the Engineering activities are found in the [Professional Skills tab](https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=60820&section=4).

You will receive a number of assignments through the term, some optional recorded video lectures, have lectures on Tuesdays and tutorials on Fridays, and have the opportunity to talk one-on-one with our teaching assistants on three days during term. It will be easy to lose track of all the material, so the [Calendar of Events](https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=60820&section=1) tab is the hub around which everything else revolves. **Here you can see at a glance what happens each day**, including assignments, lectures, tutorials and the release of optional video lectures. All the active events in the calendar are linked directly to the activities themselves, so you should be able to find everything easily.

**Task numbering**

- There are five CS Assignments, numbered CA1 to CA5. Assignments CA1, CA2 and CA3 are to give you essential practice. Assignments CA4 (Tetris - worth 20%) and CA5 (Pacman specification - worth 15%) are assessed courseworks.
- Assignments will usually be acommpanied by a video explaining your task. For example, the video introducing CS assignment 4 will be video CA4.0. Additional videos related to this assignment will be numbered CA4.1, CA4.2, etc.
- There is a [course github repository](https://github.com/UCL-ENGF0034-2026/course-materials) containing all the assignments, source code from the lectures, and any additional accompanying material.
- The Engineering faculty-led activities are:

- Pebble in the pond
- Teamwork, leadership and management
- Ethics
- Presentation skills
- Careers & Employability

The assessed pieces are Presentations (term 2 reading week, worth 10%) and Ethics report (due 26th Feb 2021, worth 15%). Details of these activities can be found on the [Professional Skills tab](https://moodle.ucl.ac.uk/course/view.php?id=60820&section=4). Scenarios (led by [Prof. James Cole](https://profiles.ucl.ac.uk/32379-james-cole)) worth 40% will take place in term 2 - more details on this will come closer to the time.

### Week 1 - Pebble in the Pond

The idea for Pebble in the Pond came from thinking about impact we have as Engineers and Scientists. The Engineering Faculty’s motto is Change the World because Science and Technology have such a big and obvious impact on the world around us. There are the noticeable, mobile phones, cars and vaccines and the more obscure, toothpaste, toys and beer. We, as Scientists and Engineers have to be aware of that impact as well as the fact that our actions can have surprising consequences. As the people of Karlskorg found out when they changed the order they cleared their roads of snow and ended up reducing their healthcare costs. So how does this get us to an icebreaker activity? Well, we wanted a fun and engaging way to introduce this idea to our students right at the beginning of their degree programmes. What was a bit like the impact an engineer or scientist would have on society – a pebble dropping into a pond and the ripples travelling through the water. How would the pebble get there? Our students would work in teams and those teams would work together to build a way of moving the pebble. Engineering and Science aren’t solo activities and this would be a great way of introducing that concept – one that runs throughout the teaching in the faculty. Also, it sounded like a lot of fun. In fact, it is – here’s a video from 2015 which shows you how fun this is.

#### Teamwork Lives and Dies by Good Communication

**This film was shown in the teamwork sessions.**

In previous years the most frequently used criterion for IPAC (Individual Contribution to Teamwork) rubrics was been 'communication'. It has often been treated as if communication is simple act of sending a message to another person. **It is more complex than that, much more complex...**

[embedded content]

**
**

**Does your own cultural background influence the way that you communicate with others? **

Read the introductory paragraph below and then take the Harvard University test to see if you have any hidden communication biases.

At UCL you will get a lot of excellent experience of working in teams that are very diverse in cultural backgrounds, skills, personal backgrounds, abilities and qualities. This is what makes teams more able than individuals to respond creatively to fast-paced changing environments and difficult problems. Yet, a diversity of backgrounds, personalities and abilities can lead to unintentional miscommunications and exclusion of individuals who do not fit in with the teams way of doing things. Research in recent years has shown that most people have some unconscious biases (also called Implicit Associations) which they are not aware of. These are hidden underlying attitudes or stereotypes that you hold about certain groups of people, which influence the way you understand and engage with that group or person.

Take this [Harvard University Test](https://implicit.harvard.edu/implicit/takeatest.html) to find out if you have any unconscious biases. You will need to read the preliminary information on the landing page and then proceed to the test page. Here you will see a list of different tests - take the Race IAT (IAT means Implicit Association Test)

Reflect on the results of your test. Were they surprising? It is common for people to find unconscious biases that they did not know they held. It is important that we all become aware of these and in doing so change the way we engage and communicate with diverse groups of people.

#### Essential Guidance

##### Providing feedback on your assessed work

Feedback concerning your work is an extremely important part of your academic development at UCL, and the Department is committed to providing appropriate support. We aim to ensure that the assessment mechanisms allow students to demonstrate the skills and knowledge they have gained and that the assessments are carried out fairly and consistently. It is a priority of the Department to provide students with suitably instructive and timely feedback. Late submission penalties are given in the [Academic Manual Section 3.12](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/academic-manual/chapters/chapter-4-assessment-framework-taught-programmes/section-3-module-assessment#3.12)

##### Turnaround time

The Department aims to return assessed work within the period outlined in the [Academic Manual Section 5.2.4](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/academic-manual/chapters/chapter-4-assessment-framework-taught-programmes/section-5-assessment-feedback#5.2) The feedback turnaround times are monitored by theDepartmental Teaching Committee, and we expect students to have had the opportunity to reflect, and act, on their learning from the feedback in subsequent assessments.

#### Recognising Feedback

During the course of your studies on the module it is important to note that you will not only get feedback on your assessed work but instead the feedback you receive from teaching staff will come in many shapes and sizes.

These pieces of feedback may range from replies to your questions in the Q&A Forum, comments from tutors on forum posts, verbal feedback in face-to-face meetings and teaching sessions to name but a few.

**Feed Forward**

It's important that you recognise when you are receiving this feedback and that you apply it, so it feeds forward into future pieces of work.

#### Research and Analysis

##### [image: Concept of flow chart]

##### [Workflow and Tools](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/workflow-and-tools)

What tools do you need to do research efficiently, and why it is important that you choose tools that will work together across your devices? This lesson talks you through how to make these important choices so that you can work efficiency from the start.

##### [[image: Computer screen showing book shelves.]Information Sources]( https://www.explaining-the-future.org/information_sources)

Even experienced researchers sometimes neglect useful sources of information, either because they forget about them or they never knew they existed in the first place. This lesson will remind you of the basic sources you should know, some tricks in using them efficiently, and introduce you to a few new ones.

[image: Cogwheels showing different types of tools, sources, and activities that might be done in a research project.]

##### [Research Process](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/research_process)

Finding information and understanding its importance takes time and involves various stages of work. This lesson will explain these stages and why important to get too lost in the details before you really understand where your work fits into the landscape.

##### [image: Desk with laptop showing a complex spreadsheet.]Analysis

To determine whether a technology is likely to be successful, you must define various criteria for its success. _R__ead Sunny's guidance on the subject in **Chapter 4 of**[Explaining the Future,](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/etfucldirectlink) available electronically to the UCL community._

#### Communication

##### [[image: Presentation audience being distracted by their devices and each other.]](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/audience_and_explanation)[Audience and Explanation](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/audience_and_explanation)

Many people forget that communication is a two-way process. This lesson applies communication theory to how get technical ideas across, and provides practical steps to help you figure out how best to help your audience understand your work.

##### [[image: Trying to fit a square peg in a round hole.]Technical Argument]( https://www.explaining-the-future.org/technical_argument)

To explain your work and show that you've done something worthwhile, you need to start by making clear why the problem you were working on was worth solving, what exactly needed to be solved. This lesson provides a formula to help you to create arguments without missing out important steps.

##### [[image: Hand with red pen editing typed paper.]Outlining and Feedback]( https://www.explaining-the-future.org/outlining-and-feedback)

A problem in the writing process is that feedback usually comes too late. In this lesson we explain how to put together a good outline and get feedback on it in a way that is painless for both you and the person helping you. This way, you will already be on your second draft by the time you start writing.

##### [[image: Road sign seen against the background of the sky with the word "Original" with an arrow pointing right and "Copy with an arrow pointing left.]Referencing, Plagiarism, and AI]( https://www.explaining-the-future.org/referencing_and_plagiarism)

Just as the internet makes it easy to cut and paste other's text into your own work, universities have tools that make this kind of cheating easy to spot. In this lesson we show you that you can steal as many words and ideas as you want as long as you quote and reference properly.

#### Visual Presentation

##### [[image: Brain thinking about pair of eyes with the legend: People think visually.]]( https://www.explaining-the-future.org/visualisation)[Visualisation](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/visualisation)

Diagrams, pictures, and graphs are all powerful tools for getting your technical ideas across, both in papers and presentations. In this lesson we teach you some rules to help you create effective diagrams that are appropriate for your audience.

##### [[image: Picture of a speaker standing in front of a projected image talking into a microphone.]]( https://www.explaining-the-future.org/presentations)[Presentations](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/presentations)

This lesson covers the basics of giving a clear and reasoned argument using readable, coherent slides, and preparing for the performance you will have to give on the day.

##### [[image: A comic-book style page explaining the features of a graphic novel.]](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/posters)[Posters](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/posters)

This lesson will explain how to design a poster that is both legible and easy to follow. It encourages you to think of a poster as a comic book or graphic novel: heavy on pictures, light on text, and designed so that it is clear what to read next, as well as giving other tips on typography, titles, and pictures.

#### Writing

##### [[image: A wall of yellow blocks with the word writing across it.]](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/building_text)[Building Text](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/building_text)

Writing is just like everything else: if you do it systematically it is not easy, but straightforward. Here we will look at how following simple structural rules when writing sentences, paragraphs, sections, and chapters can make it easy for the reader to follow.

##### [[image: Photograph of part of a dictionary page with the definition of the word credibility.]]( https://www.explaining-the-future.org/credibility)[Credibility](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/credibility)

There are lots subtle ways in which we can gain, or lose, the confidence of our readers. In this lesson we go into what these are and provide some rules that will help ensure you keep the trust of your reader even if they are not pre-disposed to agree with your argument.

##### [[image: Two executives looking over a report.]]( https://www.explaining-the-future.org/executive-summaries)[Executive Summaries](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/executive-summaries)

Whether you're writing your own report or have been asked to evaluate someone else's an executive summary is an important and powerful document. This lesson will teach you what it is and how to write one.

##### [[image: Flaming at symbol]](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/e-mail)[Writing Effective E-mails](https://www.explaining-the-future.org/e-mail)

Poorly written e-mails can greatly reduce your own personal productivity and that of your team. This lesson introduces you to some of the psychology of e-mail and the mechanics of writing them well.

General Specification of the Program to Write
You should remember or review the lecture content about the simple robot abstraction (Week
2 on Moodle). The coursework is to implement a drawing program that displays and animates
a robot moving around a rectangular maze, starting at the entrance and finishing at the exit.
The program should use the drawing app, which supports foreground and background layers,
and can draw polygon shapes (such as a triangle).
As an example, a maze in the drawing window might look like this (this is an example, you
don’t have to use this maze):

--- Page 4 ---
4
Here the background layer displays the maze, with the filled squares representing the internal
maze walls, while the grey filled square is a reflective marker denoting the exit. The robot is on
the foreground layer at the maze entrance and is represented by the green triangle pointing in
the direction of movement (to the right, or east in this case).
When the program runs the robot moves through the maze to try and find the marker at the
exit.
The maze and the exit marker are drawn once at the start of the program and remain
unchanged on the background layer. The robot is moved around the foreground layer,
representing the animation of the robot running through the maze.
The robot is simple and only these functions should be provided to control the robot:
• forward() – move forward to the next square in the direction the robot is facing. If
there is a maze wall in front of the robot it does not move.
• left() – turn the robot direction left (anti-clockwise) by 90 degrees, while remaining in
the same position.
• right() – turn the robot direction right (clockwise) by 90 degrees, while remaining in the
same position.
• int atMarker() – return true if the robot is on the exit marker, otherwise false.
• int canMoveForward() – return true if the robot can move forward as there is no maze
wall in front of it. Return false otherwise.
The robot cannot move diagonally or turn through any other angle than 90 degrees. You can
additionally add parameters to these functions, to pass in the information about the robot
position and direction, and for forward, left, right return a value if needed.
Maze Rules: All mazes, whether designed by hand, read from a data file or generated by your
program, should follow these rules:
• The maze is a rectangular grid of equal-sized squares. Each square is either empty, a
wall, or the exit marker.
• Squares are identified by (x, y) coordinates, where x is the column counting from the
left and y is the row counting from the top, so (0, 0) is the top-left square.
• The maze is surrounded by an outer wall one square thick, except for exactly one
entrance and one exit, each a single-square gap in the outer wall.

--- Page 5 ---
5
• The exit marker occupies the exit square. The robot starts on the entrance square,
facing into the maze.
• There must be at least one path of empty squares from the entrance to the exit,
moving only horizontally or vertically between adjacent squares.
• Any square outside the grid is treated as a wall, so canMoveForward returns false and
the robot can never leave the maze.
• Mazes may contain dead ends and loops. A simple maze for Stage 3 might have no
loops, but a more general search algorithm must not get trapped in one.
• The maze can be any size, provided the whole maze fits in the drawing window. The
drawing window can be resized to make it bigger.
The Program to Write
The program can be written in stages as suggested in the list below. Go as far as you can, but
being able to complete the basic stages will be good enough to get a pass mark if you write
reasonable code.
Basic Stage 1: Display a maze in the drawing window. The maze can be one that you have
designed, it doesn’t need to be generated by code. You might read the maze structure from a
data file.
Basic Stage 2: Display a robot and animate it so that it moves through the maze to the exit
marker. The robot can follow a path that you have pre-determined, it does not need to use a
maze path finding algorithm.
Stage 3: Implement a basic maze search algorithm to move the robot from the entrance to the
exit marker. Start with something simple, for example a maze where the robot can always turn
right to get to the exit. Then progressively try more complicated mazes, where the search
algorithm gets more sophisticated. Think about using recursion.
Stage 4: Implement an algorithm to generate mazes, with a single entrance and single exit.
(challenging)
Stage 5: Improve your robot search algorithm to work with any maze you can generate.
(challenging)

A drawing program can’t conveniently do input from the keyboard as it cannot display
input prompts that the user can see. All output to stdout is redirected to the drawapp
program, so prompts will be redirected as well and the drawapp program will treat
them as invalid input.
However, you can use command line arguments. For example:
./a.out 0 1 east | java -jar drawapp-5.0.jar
Here the “0 1 east” are the command line arguments to the program, meaning the
robot starts at coordinate (0, 1) in the maze, facing east.
To access the command line arguments the main function has two
parameters:
argc – the argument count, which is the number of command line arguments
given including the name of the program. Hence, for ‘./a.out 0 1 east’ the value
of argc will be 4.
argv – a pointer to an array of pointers to C Strings, hence of type char **. Each
string holds one of the command line arguments and the size of the array of
pointers will be 4, indexed 0-3. A command line argument is always stored as a
string even if it represents a number.
This section of code illustrates how to use argc and argv:

{
// The default values if the command line arguments

int initialX = 0;
int initialY = 1;
char *initialDirection = "east";
